ギター が ひけます か — Can you play the guitar?
You learn the dictionary form of verbs (たべる, かく, する) and use it to say what you can do (～こと が できます), what your hobby is (しゅみ は ～こと です) and what you do before something else (～まえ に).
I can, I’m able; it’s done, it’s ready
I collect, I gather (→ あつめる)
not easily, not very (+ neg.); quite
Before going to bed I read a book.
To form the dictionary form (the “plain” form) from the ～ます form, for every group.
To say what you can do: ～こと が できます / X が できます.
To introduce your hobby: しゅみ は ～こと です.
To say what you do before something: ～る まえ に / X の まえ に.
To ask at a hotel or shop whether you can pay by card, book, etc.
Yuki helps Ana call a traditional inn in Kyoto to make a booking for the autumn trip.
Yes, Sakura Inn, how may I help you?
Hello, my name is Ana, from Spain. I’d like to make a booking.
Thank you very much. For when?
From the fifth of November, for five days, two people.
I see. Is it possible to have dinner in the room?
Yes, it is. It’s a full Japanese set meal. Is there anyone who can’t eat meat?
No, we can both eat anything.
The bath can be used until eleven at night.
Er, is there anyone who can speak English?
Only a little. But your Japanese is really very good.
No, I still have a lot to learn. I practised a lot before calling.
Then we look forward to seeing you.
“koto ga dekimasu” = it’s possible, I can
I still have a lot to learn
(very polite) “omachi shite orimasu” = we look forward to seeing you
Group 1 verbs end in -u: かく, よむ, はなす, まつ. With “tsu” (まつ) and “su” (はなす), the final u is barely heard.
All group 2 verbs end in -る: たべる, みる, ねる. る is a soft “r”, between r and l.
Very polite phone phrases: go-za-i-mas, moh-shi-mas. The final u disappears.
1. The dictionary form: the “basic” form of the verb
So far you’ve only used the polite ～ます form. In the dictionary, though, verbs appear in their plain form (たべる, not たべます). You need it for many grammar structures. Here it is for each group:
the -i sound before ます becomes -u
Group 1: the “i” row of the hiragana table moves to the “u” row: き→く, ぎ→ぐ, し→す, ち→つ, に→ぬ, び→ぶ, み→む, り→る, い→う.
Careful: かいます → かう (not “かいう”), あります → ある. And きます (to come) → くる, a completely different form!
2. I can…: ～こと が できます
The dictionary form + こと turns the verb into a noun (“the act of…”). Then you say that this thing “can be done” (できます):
The short version, with a noun: X が できます. ピアノ が できます (I can play the piano), にほんご が できます (I can speak Japanese).
できます covers both “I can” (I’m able) and “it’s possible” (it’s allowed). Context decides.
3. Your hobby: しゅみ は ～こと です
For hobbies: しゅみ は (my hobby is) + verb in the dictionary form + こと です.
My hobby is cooking. (with a noun)
To be more specific, add details: しゅみ は にほん の きって を あつめる こと です (My hobby is collecting Japanese stamps).
X の まえ に
にねん まえ に、スペイン へ きました。 (two years ago)
The verb before まえ に is ALWAYS in the dictionary form, even if everything is in the past: にほん へ いく まえ に、にほんご を べんきょう しました. Not “いった まえ に”!

クラブ の しゅみ — The club’s hobbies
Yuki asked every club member what their hobby is and what they can do.
Carlos’s hobby is watching anime. He can watch anime in Japanese without subtitles.
But he can’t read kanji at all yet.
Sofia can play the piano. She’s been playing since she was five.
Hanako’s hobby is dancing flamenco. She takes lessons every Saturday.
Mrs Suzuki’s hobby is growing flowers in her garden.
Kenji is best at cooking, but his hobby is fishing.
Mihai likes playing the guitar and collecting old photos.
My hobby is… asking everyone about their hobbies!
ふるい しゃしん — The old photo
Mihai’s hobby is collecting old photos.
On Sunday mornings he likes going to the flea market in Madrid.
At the market you find all sorts of old things. Old radios, old clocks, old books…
One Sunday, Mihai found a box at a small stall.
There were lots of photos in the box.
Most of them were photos of Spain. But just one was different.
It was a photo from Japan. A young woman in a kimono was standing under a cherry tree.
Something was written on the back of the photo.
Mihai can read hiragana. But there were lots of kanji and he couldn’t read it all.
“Excuse me, how much is this photo?” “Five euros.”
On Friday, before the club, Mihai showed the photo to Yuki.
Yuki read the back of the photo.
“March 1970. In Kyoto. From Michiko, to José.”
At that moment, Mrs Suzuki came into the room.
Mrs Suzuki looked at the photo and froze.
“My name is Suzuki Michiko. When I was young, I met a Spanish student called José.”
“José was studying Japanese painting in Kyoto.”
“Before he went back to Spain, I gave him this photo.”
“Then I came to Spain too. I married José.”
“He passed away last year. I sold a lot of his things. And this photo… I sold it by mistake.”
Tears fell from Mrs Suzuki’s eyes.
Mihai put the photo in Mrs Suzuki’s hands.
“It was only five euros. Your nikujaga is worth much more.”
Mrs Suzuki laughed through her tears.
That evening, Mihai wrote in his notebook:
“Before going to Japan, I want to learn more kanji. So that I can read the important things.”
Then he picked up his guitar and played a quiet song.
In the next room, the white kitten was listening.
Mrs Suzuki still keeps the photo on her desk. Every day she looks at it and smiles.
Where did Mihai find the photo?
Who is the woman in the photo?
What does Mihai want to do before going to Japan?
